newsitem.title: USA: Revised Miami budget falls short on reserves.
newsitem.headline: Revised Miami budget falls short on reserves.

text.p: Miami City Commission drafted a revised budget that uses land sale proceeds to close a deficit, but falls well short of the reserve requirements set by a state oversight board.

The budget was approved by the commission late Thursday and will go before the oversight board for approval on Monday. Unless the oversight board approves a Miami budget by Feb 1, the city will be barred from spending any money, except for paying debt service on bonds, without board permission.
On Jan 14, the oversight board rejected the first budget the city submitted, saying $9.9 million of the $275 million in revenues the city budgeted for were "too iffy" to count on.

The revised plan would raise about $16.5 million by accelerating the sale of five city-owned buildings and lots. They include the little-used Bobby Maduro Stadium, a maintenance building near Jackson Memorial Hospital, a downtown office building and two downtown lots that had been considered for parking garages.

The budget does not include proceeds from the sale of several more valuable properties the city may sell, such as the Miami Springs Golf Course and the bayfront land the county wants for seaport expansion. Mayor Joe Carollo said the city wants to avoid "a fire sale" on those properties.

Police Chief Donald Warshaw also said he expects written confirmation before Monday from the U.S. Justice Department that the city will receive a $3 million police grant. That revenue was among the funds whose certainty the oversight board had questioned.
If the revenues can be counted on, the new budget would close the city's $68 million deficit for the year that began Oct 1, and leave about $6.9 million in reserves.

When it rejected the earlier plan, the oversight board asked the city to set aside $13.6 million of unallocated funds, or 20 percent of the estimated deficit, in reserves against uncollected funds or emergencies.

Under questioning by Carollo, City Attorney A. Quinn Jones told commissioners they were not legally obliged to come up with any reserves. He said the city's agreement with the oversight board only required it to close the deficit.
Chuck Wolfe, chief of staff for the oversight board, disagreed. He said the agreement "gives the oversight board in its sole discretion the ability to approve or reject the plan."
Carollo, who has strongly criticized the oversight board as too harsh, hinted at legal action if the board rejects the latest budget because of the reserve requirement.
"If it's turned down for those reasons I assure you we will have ample rights to get satisfaction through the courts," Carollo told the Miami Herald.

Gov. Lawton Chiles appointed the oversight board in December to guide Miami to fiscal solvency. The $68 million deficit for the current fiscal year was discovered after three top officials resigned to face corruption charges.
Chiles appointed the board under a state law that also gives him the authority to take over the city if he feels that is warranted.
